newsitem.title: INDIA: India's IOC says borrowings enough for oil needs.
newsitem.headline: India's IOC says borrowings enough for oil needs.

text.p: India's state-run Indian Oil Corp's (IOC) unutilised external commercial borrowing (ECB) limits were adequate to cover its needs for oil imports until June, company officials said on Monday.
"Our ECB cap is $2.9 billion. We have not reached the cap and the current ECB is hovering around $2.0 billion," the official, who did not want to be identified, told Reuters.
"We see no problem till June," he said.
State-controlled IOC is the main distributing agency of refined products, some of which are sold to Indian consumers at heavily subsidised prices.
IOC, Oil and Natural Gas Corp, Hindustan Petroleum Corp Ltd and Bharat Petroleum Corp Ltd are owed around 160 billion ($4.4 billion) by the government for selling at subsidised prices.
Money owed to IOC accounts for around two thirds of the total oil pool deficit, effectively the amount the government owes oil companies for selling products well below world prices.
The IOC official said world crude prices were on a downward trend and currently ruling around $17 per tonne, the same level as a year ago.
"We are not expecting any problem on the imports front," he said.
Indian corporates need government sanction before they can borrow abroad.
The official said the government had earlier put a cap of $2.0 billion on the company's external commercial borrowings. It was recently raised to $2.9 billion, he said.
IOC raises funds through short-term syndicated loans of 180 days to finance imports of crude and petroleum products, company officials said. It is one of the largest such borrowers in the country.
Analysts expect the government to announce a hike in petroleum product prices in the coming weeks or soon after the start of the new fiscal year in April.
The government last raised prices in July, when it had only been in power a month, but that adjustment was soon rendered inadequate by a surge in world prices to six year highs.
The subsequent delay in raising prices again has caused the oil deficit to reach worrying proportions.
The handicap of carrying the cost has forced India's oil companies to borrow heavily.
India's crude oil output in 1996/97 (April-March) is forecast at around 34 million tonnes, down from 35.19 million in 1995/96.
The country's demand for petroleum products is forecast to go up to about 81 million tonnes in the year ending March 31, 1997 from 74.7 million in 1995/96.
